# stash branch: turn a stash into a real branch

After this page you can recover WIP that sat in the stash while `main` moved, by running `git stash branch`, and explain why that beats `stash apply` on a divergent tip.

## Thesis

`git stash` saves dirty work and resets to HEAD. If you then commit on the same branch, `stash apply` can conflict against new commits. **`git stash branch <name>`** creates a new branch starting at the commit the stash was based on, checks it out, applies the stash, and drops the stash entry on success. Your WIP lands on a clean line of history.

Basics of stash push/pop live in the earlier stash chapter; this page is only the branch escape hatch.

Verified with **git 2.47.3**.

## Mental model

```text
  stash created at commit B
  main later moves to C

  stash apply on C  →  often conflicts

  stash branch rescue
       │
       ▼
  new branch at B + stash applied + stash dropped
```

## Lab

<!-- file: stash-branch-lab.sh -->
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/sb-demo && mkdir /tmp/sb-demo && cd /tmp/sb-demo
git init -b main
git config user.name t
git config user.email t@t
echo base > f.txt && git add f.txt && git commit -m base
echo dirty > f.txt
git stash push -m wip
echo other > g.txt && git add g.txt && git commit -m other
git stash branch rescue-stash
git status -sb
git log --oneline --decorate
cat f.txt
git stash list
```

Verified output:

```text
Switched to a new branch 'rescue-stash'
On branch rescue-stash
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   f.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
Dropped refs/stash@{0} (c40428c4766e3562e7dde6f0c873f2ecee356820)
=== status ===
## rescue-stash
 M f.txt
?? out.txt
=== log ===
12fb4d8 (HEAD -> rescue-stash) base
=== f.txt ===
dirty
=== stash list ===
```

The branch `rescue-stash` sits on `base` with `f.txt` restored to `dirty`. The stash entry is gone. Commit `other` remains on `main` only.

## When to use it

- You stashed to pull/rebase, then realized the WIP belongs on its own branch.
- Apply conflicts look worse than restarting from the stash base.
- An agent left a stash and you want an isolatable review branch.

## Pitfalls

1. Expecting `stash branch` to keep the stash on failure — on success it drops; on failure it usually leaves the stash.
2. Naming collision with an existing branch.
3. Stash that included untracked files (`stash -u`) — confirm with `git stash show --include-untracked` before branching.
4. Using stash as long-term storage — prefer real commits on a WIP branch.

## Summary

- `git stash branch <name> [<stash>]` rebuilds a branch from the stash base and applies the stash.
- Prefer it when the original tip has moved and apply conflicts.
- Still commit or discard promptly — stashes are not backups.


## Worked scenarios

### Scenario A — agent left a stash mid-task
```bash
git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{0}
git stash branch agent/wip stash@{0}
```

Review on `agent/wip`, commit or discard, delete the branch when done.

### Scenario B — stash includes untracked files
```bash
git stash push -u -m 'wip with new files'
git stash branch recover
```

Confirm new files appear after branching.

### Scenario C — compare to apply
If `git stash apply` conflicts heavily after `main` moved, abort the apply (`git merge --abort` if needed / reset), then `stash branch` from the still-present stash entry.

## Relation to the main stash chapter

Keep using `stash push` / `pop` / `apply` for short switches. Graduate to `stash branch` when the WIP deserves history.

## Common mistakes (extended)

- Dropping the stash manually before branching.
- Branching from the wrong stash index (`stash@{2}`).
- Leaving rescue branches forever — prune after merge.
